```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6,
                      fig.height = 2.8, dpi = 96)
```

A factorial survey shows each respondent a few short descriptions --
*vignettes* -- whose attributes are varied by design, and asks for a rating
or a yes/no answer. Because the attributes are assigned experimentally, their
effects can be estimated cleanly, and when one attribute is a cost, they can
be expressed as willingness to pay.

This vignette walks through the workflow with take-away lunch boxes as the
example: designing the vignettes, deciding how many respondents are needed,
and analysing real ratings.

```{r setup}
library(FactorialSurvey)
```

## 1. Design the vignettes

List the attributes and their levels. Levels may be text or numbers; every
level of every attribute will appear in the design.

```{r design}
attrs <- list(
  main  = c("grilled fish", "teriyaki chicken", "tofu hamburger"),
  side  = c("no", "yes"),
  info  = c("no", "yes"),
  price = c(700, 900, 1100, 1300)
)

design <- fs_defficient(attrs, n_vignettes = 16, n_blocks = 2,
                        seed = 1, verbose = FALSE)
design
```

The D-efficiency is reported relative to an orthogonal design of the same
size, so 100 percent is the best attainable. `fs_efficiency()` computes the
same measure for any design, including ones built elsewhere; pass the
intended levels so that a level that never appears is caught.

```{r efficiency}
fs_efficiency(design)
```

Respondents are then given blocks and presentation orders that balance
carryover, and the rows are turned into the text shown on screen.

```{r assign}
design <- fs_vignette_text(
  design,
  "A {{main}} lunch box, side dish: {{side}}, nutrition label: {{info}}, ",
  column = "part1"
)
schedule <- fs_assign(design, n_respondents = 200, seed = 1)
head(schedule[, c("respondent", "block", "position", "main", "price")])
```

`fs_export()` writes the design or schedule for a survey platform, for
example as a Qualtrics Loop & Merge table.

## 2. Decide how many respondents you need

Before fielding, simulate the survey under plausible effects -- from a pilot
or a similar study -- and see how often each effect would be detected and how
precise the willingness to pay would be.

```{r power}
pw <- fs_power(
  design, n_respondents = c(50, 150),
  coef = c("(Intercept)" = 1, "mainteriyaki chicken" = 0.7,
           "maintofu hamburger" = 0.1, sideyes = 0.3, infoyes = 0.15,
           price = -0.0015),
  formula = ~ main + side + info + price, price = "price",
  n_sim = 50, seed = 1, verbose = FALSE
)
pw[pw$term %in% c("sideyes", "infoyes"), ]
```

A modest effect such as the nutrition label is easily missed with 50
respondents. `mwtp_relative` is the half-width of the confidence interval as a share of
the true value: 0.3 means roughly plus or minus 30 percent. Use more
simulations (200 or more) for a final decision.

## 3. Analyse the ratings

The `bento` data hold real ratings of eight lunch-box vignettes by 48
students, on a 0 to 10 purchase-intention scale.

```{r data}
head(bento)
```

`fs_betareg()` fits a beta regression, which respects the bounds of the
rating scale. Each student rated eight vignettes, so the ratings of one
person are correlated; `cluster` makes the standard errors robust to this.

```{r fit}
fit <- fs_betareg(rating ~ main + side + info + price, data = bento,
                  cluster = ~ respondent, compute_me = FALSE)
summary(fit)
```

## 4. Willingness to pay

The marginal willingness to pay (MWTP) values each attribute in yen: the
price change that would offset it.

```{r mwtp}
w <- fs_mwtp(fit, price = "price")
w
plot(w)
```

The expected willingness to pay (EWTP) values a whole lunch box -- a complete
scenario -- rather than a single attribute.

```{r ewtp}
boxes <- data.frame(
  main = c("grilled fish", "teriyaki chicken", "teriyaki chicken"),
  side = c(0, 0, 1),
  info = c(0, 0, 1),
  row.names = c("Fish, plain", "Chicken, plain", "Chicken, full")
)
e <- fs_ewtp(fit, boxes, price = "price")
e
plot(e) + ggplot2::labs(x = "Expected willingness to pay (yen)")
```

## 5. Yes/no responses

When respondents answer whether they would accept a scenario at the stated
cost, `fs_logit()` takes the place of `fs_betareg()`, and `fs_mwtp()` and
`fs_ewtp()` work in the same way. Simulated data illustrate it here.

```{r logit}
yesno <- fs_simulate_ratings(
  design, n_respondents = 300,
  coef = c("(Intercept)" = 2, "mainteriyaki chicken" = 0.7,
           "maintofu hamburger" = 0.1, sideyes = 0.3, infoyes = 0.1,
           price = -0.002),
  formula = ~ main + side + info + price, response = "binary",
  name = "buy", seed = 2
)
lfit <- fs_logit(buy ~ main + side + info + price, data = yesno,
                 cluster = ~ respondent, compute_me = FALSE)
fs_mwtp(lfit, price = "price")
```
